segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now about the times and the seasons, brothers and sisters, you have no need for anything to be written to you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord comes just like a thief in the night.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When people are saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Peace and security,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: then sudden destruction comes upon them, like labor pains upon a pregnant woman, and they will certainly not escape.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, brothers and sisters, are not in darkness, so that the day should overtake you like a thief,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for you are all children of light and children of the day. We do not belong to night or to darkness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, let us not sleep as the rest do, but let us stay awake and be sober.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk are drunk at night.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and as a helmet the hope of salvation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God did not appoint us for wrath but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as you are in fact doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we ask you, brothers and sisters, to recognize those who labor among you and lead you in the Lord and admonish you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to hold them in the very highest regard in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And we urge you, brothers and sisters: admonish the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with everyone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good, both for one another and for everyone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rejoice always,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: pray without ceasing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: give thanks in everything; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not quench the Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: do not treat prophecies with contempt,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but test everything; hold on to what is good,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: hold back from every kind of evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now may the God of peace himself make you holy through and through, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole and without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, pray for us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet all the brothers and sisters with a holy kiss.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I put you under oath before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers and sisters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and the letter is plainly meant for the whole congregation (see verse 27). 'Brothers' alone now suggests to an English reader that only men are addressed. Several modern translations make the same choice; others keep 'brothers' with a footnote.

The phrase comes from Israel's prophets (for example Amos 5 and Joel 2), where it names the day God acts decisively in judgment and rescue. Paul uses it for the coming of Jesus as Lord, which he has just described at the end of the previous chapter.

Many scholars hear an echo of Roman imperial propaganda, which advertised peace and security as the benefits of Roman rule; Thessalonica was a city that prized its ties to Rome. Others see only an allusion to the false prophets who cried 'Peace' when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). The two are not mutually exclusive, and the question remains debated.

notes.traditional: children of light / sons of light
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'sons of light and sons of day', a Semitic idiom in which 'son of X' means a person who belongs to X or is characterized by it. The expression 'sons of light' is known from Jewish writings of the period, including the Dead Sea Scrolls. 'Children' is used because the whole congregation is addressed.

notes.phrase: the breastplate of faith and love
notes.note: The image draws on Isaiah 59:17, where God himself puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation. Paul applies the armor to believers and attaches to it his familiar triad of faith, love and hope.

notes.phrase: whether we are awake or asleep
notes.note: These are the same two verbs used in verses 6–7 for moral alertness and moral stupor, but most interpreters take them here to mean 'alive or dead' at the Lord's coming, picking up the concern of 4:13–18 about believers who have died. A minority reads the words in the same moral sense as in verse 6, which sits awkwardly with the exhortation there. The translation keeps the same English words so the reader can see the echo.

The Greek verb can mean either 'stand at the head of, lead' or 'care for, give aid to', and both senses are well attested in the period. Standing between 'labor' and 'admonish', it may describe practical care and patronage as much as authority; some translations render it 'care for you'. No formal office is named.

The word means 'out of order, undisciplined', used for example of soldiers who break ranks. Many modern versions translate 'idle' because 2 Thessalonians 3:6–11 uses related words of people who refuse to work, and some papyri use the word group for absence from work. The word itself is broader than laziness, however, so the general sense is kept here; older English versions had 'unruly'.

The Greek noun can mean either 'outward appearance' or 'kind, sort'. The King James Version took the first sense ('abstain from all appearance of evil'), which has often been understood as avoiding anything that merely looks wrong. Most scholars and modern translations take it as 'kind' or 'form', which fits the contrast with 'what is good' in the previous verse. The two commands use related verbs in Greek, reflected here in 'hold on to' and 'hold back from'.

The Greek word means both arrival and presence, and in the period it was a standard term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. Readers in Thessalonica would have heard that overtone when it was used of the Lord Jesus.

notes.phrase: I put you under oath before the Lord
notes.traditional: I charge you by the Lord / I adjure you by the Lord
notes.note: The letter shifts here from 'we' to 'I', which suggests Paul adding a closing line in his own person. The verb is a strong one, binding the recipients by oath with the Lord as witness. Letters were read aloud to the gathered congregation, and Paul insists that no one be left out.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translations split between 'brothers' and 'brothers and sisters'; it needs one policy, including when a male-only sense applies.

Translations vary between 'sanctify', 'make holy' and 'consecrate', and the choice should match the register's handling of ἅγιος.
